newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin calls Solana as NATO-Russia talks drag on.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin calls Solana as NATO-Russia talks drag on.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin spoke to NATO Secretary General Javier Solana by telephone on Wednesday as Russia and the Western alliance tried to finalise a pact mapping out their relations for the next century.

The Kremlin said in a brief statement that Yeltsin spoke to Solana as the NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organisation) leader held talks with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in Moscow. It gave no details.
It also said Yeltsin had spoken by telephone to Primakov, who briefed the president on the state of the negotiations in a foreign ministry mansion in central Moscow.

Solana and Primakov held an unscheduled second day of talks after spending six hours on Tuesday trying to solve differences over the document, which is also intended to address Russian fears over NATO's eastward expansion.
The talks, expected to decide whether Russia and NATO can narrow their differences in time to sign the deal in Paris on May 27, were shrouded in secrecy.
Solana arrived by car and said nothing to reporters as he entered the foreign minstry mansion where talks were being held in central Moscow. Russian officials also declined comment.
Interfax and Itar-Tass news agencies said the talks were likely to end on Wednesday afternoon and Solana would leave Moscow immediately afterwards. A statement would be issued summarising the talks.
Yeltsin says he wants to sign an agreement with NATO on May 27 and said last week the deal was "98 percent" ready.

But, anxious to limit the criticism of his communist and nationalist foes, he has also said he will not sign an unsatisfactory agreement and told Primakov to take a tough line in the sixth round of Russia-NATO talks on the pact.
Yeltsin has said repeatedly that Russia will not back NATO's plans to invite some eastern European countries to join the alliance at a summit in Madrid in July.
But he wants a deal to ensure a peaceful partnership with NATO and keep relations with the West on track.

Russia wants a say in NATO decisions and guarantees that the Western defence alliance will not station military structures and nuclear weapons on the territory of new member states. NATO is reluctant to give such written guarantees.
Primakov indicated before the talks started on Tuesday that the deal was not ready and depended largely on Solana's position."Let us wait and see what Mr Solana brings," he said.

Some Kremlin sources say Yeltsin has already decided to sign the deal on May 27 but suggest Moscow will keep up the uncertainty and anti-NATO rhetoric until the last minute to appease his opponents at home.
